lessons.title: Budgets, costing and cash flow
lessons.html:
Financial practices every manager needs

Managers in the export chain control large amounts of money: wages, packaging, electricity, transport and chemicals. Good financial practice means planning spending, controlling it and reporting on it accurately.

Budgeting

A budget is a financial plan for a period, usually a year or a season. The steps are:

  1. Estimate volumes, for example the number of cartons the packhouse expects to pack.
  2. Estimate income: volume multiplied by the packing fee or expected price.
  3. Estimate costs: fixed costs (salaries, insurance, depreciation, rent) and variable costs that change with volume (packaging, seasonal labour, electricity for cooling).
  4. Get approval and communicate the budget to those responsible.
  5. Compare actual results with the budget each month and explain variances.

A variance is the difference between budget and actual. For example, if packaging was budgeted at R1 200 000 but cost R1 350 000, the unfavourable variance is R150 000. Find the cause: higher prices, more cartons packed, or waste.

Costing

Knowing the cost per unit helps set prices and find savings. Cost per carton = total cost divided by number of cartons. If a packhouse spends R9 000 000 to pack 600 000 cartons, the cost is R15 per carton. Separating fixed and variable costs shows how cost per carton falls as volume rises, because fixed costs are spread over more cartons.

Cash flow management

Profit is not cash. A packhouse may pay wages weekly but receive payment from exporters weeks later. A cash flow forecast shows month by month when money comes in and goes out, so that overdraft or credit facilities can be arranged in advance. Practices that improve cash flow include invoicing promptly, agreeing clear payment terms, following up on overdue accounts, buying packaging close to when it is needed, and negotiating supplier terms.

lessons.title: Financial controls, tax and reporting
lessons.html:
Internal financial controls

Controls protect the business against errors, waste and fraud.

  • Segregation of duties: the person who orders goods should not be the same person who approves payment.
  • Authorisation limits: purchases above set amounts need a manager's approval.
  • Purchase orders and goods received notes: pay only for what was ordered and received.
  • Petty cash: a fixed float, receipts for every payment, regular reconciliation.
  • Stock control: regular counts of packaging and chemicals compared with records.
  • Bank reconciliation: compare the bank statement with the accounting records monthly.
  • Payroll checks: verify worker lists against clock records to prevent ghost workers.
  • Verify bank detail changes from suppliers directly by phone using known numbers.

Tax and statutory obligations

  • Income tax on business profits.
  • VAT: businesses above the registration threshold must register with SARS. The standard rate is 15 percent. Exports are generally zero-rated, but the rules and documentation requirements must be followed; an accountant should advise.
  • PAYE on employees' wages, UIF and Skills Development Levy where applicable.
  • COIDA assessments for workplace injury cover.
  • Industry and statutory levies such as PPECB fees on exports.

Keep records for the period the law requires and submit returns on time to avoid penalties.

Financial reporting

Managers should receive and understand monthly management accounts: an income statement compared with budget, a balance sheet and a cash flow report. Key measures include gross and net profit margins, cost per carton, debtor days (how long customers take to pay) and the current ratio.

Example

A cold store manager notices that electricity costs are 20 percent over budget. Analysis shows doors left open during loading and defrost settings never adjusted. Fixing these brings costs back towards budget and improves the cold chain at the same time.

Key points

  • Budgets plan income and costs; variances must be explained.
  • Cost per unit falls as volume rises because fixed costs are spread.
  • Profit is not cash: forecast and manage cash flow.
  • Internal controls such as segregation of duties prevent fraud and errors.
  • Meet tax obligations including VAT, PAYE and UIF on time.
